summary:
Lost harvests start in the soil. Heat, drought and erosion are putting farms at risk, and the data that could help farmers is hard to use.

OrbitFarm reads your land from space. Mark your field directly on the satellite map, see simple readings on soil moisture, rain, heat and bare ground, and test how different crop sequences care for your soil. The data comes from NASA (POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, HLS, MODIS, Landsat, SRTM) and Sentinel-2.

The right crops, in the right order: OrbitFarm builds realistic alternatives to the farmer’s current rotation. It simulates each one over the last 10 years of real weather, using FAO-56 for water and RUSLE for erosion, and shows the probability that it would have improved water use, heat resilience and soil health.

Grow smarter, from space. OrbitFarm is free, bilingual (Spanish/English) and available at orbitfarm.earth.
details:
What it does

OrbitFarm helps farmers adapt their crop rotations to a changing climate using NASA satellite data. It answers one practical question: “If I change my crop rotation, will my plot do better?”

The farmer draws their plot on a satellite map and enters their current rotation: crops, order and sowing months, or an orchard with its cover crop. OrbitFarm then automatically retrieves the plot’s data: weather and solar radiation from NASA POWER, rainfall from GPM IMERG, soil moisture from SMAP, vegetation vigour (NDVI) from HLS, MODIS and Sentinel-2, surface temperature from Landsat, slope from SRTM and soil texture from SoilGrids.

How it works

OrbitFarm generates realistic alternative rotations. It starts with improvements that keep the farmer’s main crop, such as adding a legume or filling a period of bare soil, and then considers typical regional rotations. It simulates every option day by day over the last 10 years of real weather, using internationally recognised methods: the FAO-56 soil water balance for irrigation needs and RUSLE for soil erosion.

Each rotation is scored from 0 to 100 on six indicators: water, heat stress, erosion, soil health, resilience and pest break. The scores are weighted by the farmer’s own priorities. Because every rotation is simulated with the same weather, the app reports a probability of improvement: in how many of those 10 years the alternative would have outperformed the current rotation.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Turns complex satellite data into clear, plot-specific advice a farmer can act on.
  • Supports lower water use, less soil loss and better resilience to heat and drought.
  • Is honest about uncertainty: it shows how often an option would have worked, instead of claiming a single “best” answer.
  • Contributes to SDGs 2, 6, 12, 13 and 15.

Creativity

Instead of telling farmers to replace what they know, OrbitFarm first proposes small, realistic changes to their own rotation. It also lets them ask the question in reverse: choose a rotation, and the app ranks their saved plots by how well each one suits it. A 7-day, 6-week and 7-month outlook helps plan the next sowing. An AI assistant explains every result in plain language.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and Recharts.
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI and NumPy, plus Google Earth Engine for satellite processing.
  • Deployment: Docker on Google Cloud Run, at orbitfarm.earth.
  • In-app assistant: Google Gemini, with Groq as a fallback.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: free, no account needed, mobile-friendly and bilingual (English/Spanish), with a guided tutorial on every page.
  • Scientific transparency: every score can be traced back to a published formula, documented in our technical report.
  • Reliability: if one data source fails, the app switches to another.
  • Data validation: the app warns users if they draw a plot on water or an urban area.
  • Privacy: saved plots stay in the user’s browser.

We started in the Valencia region, which is our home, but the method relies on global datasets and can be extended to other regions of the world.
